steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on using Hutchinson Trace Estimation to scale physics-informed neural networks to high-dimensional and high-order PDEs: motivation, limits of existing approaches, our method and theory, experiments, and a paper outline.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- PINNs: successes and the high-dimensional/high-order cost problem
- Why high-dimensional PDEs matter; existing specialized solvers
- Existing PINN approaches for high dimensions and their limits
- Proposed method: HTE for second-order parabolic PDEs
- Theory and comparison with SDGD; extension to the biharmonic equation
- Experiments
- Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- PINNs
  - big strides on PDE problems in scientific computing, esp. low-dimensional
  - reasons: fitting capability, generalization, stability in optimization
  - but high-dimensional / high-order PDEs little explored, despite NN success on image/text data
  - main challenge: huge cost of automatic differentiation for residual loss
- High-dimensional PDEs
  - crucial; curse-of-dimensionality
  - examples: Black-Scholes (option pricing, finance), Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB, optimal control), Schrödinger (quantum physics)
  - specialized solvers: DeepBSDE, Deep Splitting Method (parabolic), algorithms for Hamilton-Jacobi equation
  - no unified, effective approach for general high-dimensional PDEs
- Existing PINN approaches
  - PINNs: versatile, arbitrary PDEs, mesh-free -> in principle not hit by curse-of-dimensionality
  - SDGD: samples dimensions to cut cost/memory per stochastic gradient; high variance when dimensions vary a lot -> hinders convergence
  - random smoothing: Gaussian noise smoothing -> less expressive, worse on non-smooth solutions
- HTE for second-order parabolic PDEs
  - Hutchinson Trace Estimation (HTE): accelerate PINNs, reduce memory
  - applies to second-order parabolic equations, biharmonic equation
  - bottleneck: full Hessian, cost quadratic in dimension
  - HTE: full Hessian -> Hessian vector product (HVP); d\times d matrix vs scalar output
  - HVP + Taylor-mode automatic differentiation in JAX -> faster, less memory
- Theory, SDGD, biharmonic
  - HTE loss converges to original PINN loss under certain conditions, unbiased
  - distinctions/similarities/applicability vs SDGD; examples; variances depend on PDE
  - more efficient in higher order/dimension -> biharmonic
  - biharmonic: fourth-order, tensor of size d^{4} with conventional PINNs
  - extend HVP to tensor-vector product (TVP): scalar output, saves memory, Taylor-mode
  - unbiased estimate for biharmonic operator; sources of variance
  - pseudocode for proper HVP/TVP implementation in JAX
- Experiments
  - HTE vs SDGD: similar convergence under same memory/speed limits, second-order nonlinear anisotropic parabolic equation; scale to 100,000 dimensions
  - accelerating Gradient-Enhanced PINN (gPINN): extra first-order derivatives of residual, HTE reduces load, keeps improvement
  - higher-order high-dimensional biharmonic equations
- Organization: Sec 2 related work, Sec 3 HTE, Sec 4 experiments, Sec 5 summary

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have made big progress in solving partial differential equation (PDE) problems in scientific computing, especially for low-dimensional equations. The reason for this is their powerful fitting capability, generalization, and stability in optimization. However, although neural networks have shown they can model high-dimensional data in the image and text domains, PINNs have not explored high-dimensional and high-order PDEs very much. The main challenge is the enormous computational cost of the automatic differentiation process that calculates the residual loss function for high-dimensional and high-order PDEs in the PINNs framework.

Solving problems with high-dimensional PDEs is crucial because of the curse-of-dimensionality, and such problems show up in various fields, for example the Black-Scholes equation in mathematical finance for option pricing, the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation in optimal control, and the Schrödinger equation in quantum physics. There are specialized high-dimensional PDE solvers for different domains, such as DeepBSDE and Deep Splitting Method for high-dimensional parabolic equations and specific algorithms for the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, but a unified and effective approach for solving general high-dimensional PDEs is missing.

PINNs is a versatile method that can handle arbitrary PDEs and is mesh-free, so in principle it is not affected by the curse-of-dimensionality. There have been recent efforts to use PINNs for high-dimensional PDEs, such as Stochastic Dimension Gradient Descent (SDGD) and random smoothing, but these approaches have limitations. SDGD tries to reduce the computational cost and memory consumption of each stochastic gradient by sampling dimensions. But when there is significant variability and variance among the dimensions, the stochastic gradients of SDGD can have substantial variance, and this hinders convergence. Random smoothing methods smooth the original neural network with Gaussian noise, which hurts the expressive power of the network and makes it less effective for non-smooth PDE solutions.

To address these limitations of PINN for high-dimensional and even high-order PDEs, we propose to use Hutchinson Trace Estimation (HTE) to accelerate PINNs and reduce the memory cost. HTE can be applied to various common PDEs, such as second-order parabolic equations and the biharmonic equation. First, for second-order parabolic PDEs, the computational bottleneck is that the entire Hessian has to be calculated, and its computational cost increases quadratically with the dimensionality. HTE is integrated into the PINNs framework to alleviate this bottleneck. Specifically, HTE turns the calculation of the entire Hessian matrix into a Hessian vector product (HVP). The full Hessian is a large matrix of dimensions d\times d, where d is the dimensionality of the PDE problem, but the output of HVP is a scalar, which reduces the memory consumption a lot. Also, HVP can use Taylor-mode automatic differentiation in JAX for rapid computation, so we get both acceleration and reduced memory usage.

- Theory, SDGD, biharmonic
  - HTE loss converges to original PINN loss under certain conditions, unbiased
  - distinctions/similarities/applicability vs SDGD; examples; variances depend on PDE
  - more efficient in higher order/dimension -> biharmonic
  - biharmonic: fourth-order, tensor of size d^{4} with conventional PINNs
  - extend HVP to tensor-vector product (TVP): scalar output, saves memory, Taylor-mode
  - unbiased estimate for biharmonic operator; sources of variance
  - pseudocode for proper HVP/TVP implementation in JAX
- Experiments
  - HTE vs SDGD: similar convergence under same memory/speed limits, second-order nonlinear anisotropic parabolic equation; scale to 100,000 dimensions
  - accelerating Gradient-Enhanced PINN (gPINN): extra first-order derivatives of residual, HTE reduces load, keeps improvement
  - higher-order high-dimensional biharmonic equations
- Organization: Sec 2 related work, Sec 3 HTE, Sec 4 experiments, Sec 5 summary

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have made big progress in solving partial differential equation (PDE) problems in scientific computing, especially for low-dimensional equations. The reason for this is their powerful fitting capability, generalization, and stability in optimization. However, although neural networks have shown they can model high-dimensional data in the image and text domains, PINNs have not explored high-dimensional and high-order PDEs very much. The main challenge is the enormous computational cost of the automatic differentiation process that calculates the residual loss function for high-dimensional and high-order PDEs in the PINNs framework.

Solving problems with high-dimensional PDEs is crucial because of the curse-of-dimensionality, and such problems show up in various fields, for example the Black-Scholes equation in mathematical finance for option pricing, the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation in optimal control, and the Schrödinger equation in quantum physics. There are specialized high-dimensional PDE solvers for different domains, such as DeepBSDE and Deep Splitting Method for high-dimensional parabolic equations and specific algorithms for the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, but a unified and effective approach for solving general high-dimensional PDEs is missing.

PINNs is a versatile method that can handle arbitrary PDEs and is mesh-free, so in principle it is not affected by the curse-of-dimensionality. There have been recent efforts to use PINNs for high-dimensional PDEs, such as Stochastic Dimension Gradient Descent (SDGD) and random smoothing, but these approaches have limitations. SDGD tries to reduce the computational cost and memory consumption of each stochastic gradient by sampling dimensions. But when there is significant variability and variance among the dimensions, the stochastic gradients of SDGD can have substantial variance, and this hinders convergence. Random smoothing methods smooth the original neural network with Gaussian noise, which hurts the expressive power of the network and makes it less effective for non-smooth PDE solutions.

To address these limitations of PINN for high-dimensional and even high-order PDEs, we propose to use Hutchinson Trace Estimation (HTE) to accelerate PINNs and reduce the memory cost. HTE can be applied to various common PDEs, such as second-order parabolic equations and the biharmonic equation. First, for second-order parabolic PDEs, the computational bottleneck is that the entire Hessian has to be calculated, and its computational cost increases quadratically with the dimensionality. HTE is integrated into the PINNs framework to alleviate this bottleneck. Specifically, HTE turns the calculation of the entire Hessian matrix into a Hessian vector product (HVP). The full Hessian is a large matrix of dimensions d\times d, where d is the dimensionality of the PDE problem, but the output of HVP is a scalar, which reduces the memory consumption a lot. Also, HVP can use Taylor-mode automatic differentiation in JAX for rapid computation, so we get both acceleration and reduced memory usage.

We also show that the loss of PINNs with HTE converges to the original PINN loss under certain conditions and that it is unbiased, which gives a solid foundation for its convergence properties. We discuss the distinctions, similarities, and applicability of HTE and SDGD, which are the most related methods. We give examples that show when HTE or SDGD is more suitable and how their variances depend on the PDE problem. After the second-order parabolic equations, we look at how HTE is even more efficient in higher-order and higher-dimensional cases, and this motivates extending HTE to the biharmonic equation.

The biharmonic equation is a fourth-order high-dimensional equation, so solving it directly with conventional PINNs would lead to a massive tensor of size d^{4}, where d is the dimensionality of the PDE problem and 4 is the order of the equation. However, if we extend the Hessian Vector Product (HVP) in HTE to a tensor-vector product (TVP), we can transform the computation of the entire huge tensor into a scalar, which is the TVP output. This saves a lot of memory and also allows rapid computation using Taylor-mode differentiation. We also show that the extended HTE method gives an unbiased estimate for the biharmonic operator, and we analyze where its variance comes from. Because it is important to implement the HVP and TVP in the HTE method in JAX properly, we give a pseudocode so that readers can get familiar with HTE and its efficient implementation.

Finally, we show the effectiveness of HTE in various experimental setups. First, we show that HTE and SDGD have similar convergence rates under the same memory constraints and speed limitations on a second-order nonlinear anisotropic parabolic equation. They successfully scale PINNs to a very high dimension (100,000 dimensions). Second, we show how HTE can accelerate the more accurate Gradient-Enhanced PINN (gPINN). gPINN needs additional first-order derivatives of the original PINN residual, so the computational load is large, but HTE reduces this burden and still keeps the improvement from gPINN. Lastly, we show the advantages of HTE for higher-order, high-dimensional biharmonic equations.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents related work. Section 3 introduces the proposed HTE method. Section 4 presents the computational experiments and Section 5 summarizes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) [1] have made significant strides in solving partial differential equation (PDE) problems in scientific computing, particularly for low-dimensional equations. This is attributed to their powerful fitting capability [2], generalization [3], and stability in optimization [4]. However, despite the demonstrated capacity of neural networks in modeling high-dimensional data in the image and text domains, the exploration of high-dimensional and high-order PDEs with PINNs has been relatively limited. The primary challenge is the enormous computational cost of the automatic differentiation process used to calculate the residual loss function for high-dimensional and high-order PDEs under the PINNs framework.

Solving high-dimensional PDE problems is crucial, considering the curse-of-dimensionality, which is prevalent in various fields, such as the Black-Scholes equation in mathematical finance for option pricing, the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation in optimal control, and the Schrödinger equation in quantum physics. Although specialized high-dimensional PDE solvers are available for different domains, such as DeepBSDE [5] and Deep Splitting Method [6] for high-dimensional parabolic equations and specific algorithms for the Hamilton-Jacobi equation [7,8], a unified and effective approach for solving general high-dimensional PDEs is lacking.

PINNs is a versatile method that can handle arbitrary PDEs and is mesh-free, so in principle it is not susceptible to the curse-of-dimensionality. Despite recent efforts to use PINNs for solving high-dimensional PDEs, such as Stochastic Dimension Gradient Descent (SDGD) [9] and random smoothing [10,11], these approaches have their limitations. SDGD attempts to reduce the computational cost and memory consumption of each stochastic gradient by sampling dimensions. However, when there is significant variability and variance among dimensions, SDGD's stochastic gradients may suffer from substantial variance, which hinders convergence. Random smoothing methods, on the other hand, smooth the original neural network with Gaussian noise, which impacts the network's expressive power and makes it less effective in handling non-smooth PDE solutions.

To address the limitations of PINN in tackling high-dimensional and even high-order PDEs, we propose the use of Hutchinson Trace Estimation (HTE) [12] to accelerate PINNs and reduce memory cost. HTE can be applied to various common PDEs, such as second-order parabolic equations and the biharmonic equation. Firstly, for second-order parabolic PDEs, the computational bottleneck is the need to calculate the entire Hessian, whose computational cost increases quadratically with the dimensionality. HTE is integrated seamlessly into the PINNs framework to alleviate this central bottleneck. Specifically, HTE transforms the calculation of the entire Hessian matrix into a Hessian vector product (HVP). Unlike the full Hessian, which is a large matrix of dimensions d\times d, where d is the dimensionality of the PDE problem, the output of HVP is a scalar, which significantly reduces memory consumption. Moreover, HVP can efficiently use Taylor-mode automatic differentiation [13] in JAX [14] for rapid computation, achieving both acceleration and reduced memory usage.

Furthermore, we show that the loss of PINNs with HTE converges to the original PINN loss under certain conditions and is unbiased, which provides a solid foundation for its convergence properties. We also discuss the distinctions, similarities, and applicability of HTE and SDGD, the most related methodologies, and we present examples illustrating when HTE or SDGD is more suitable and how their variances depend on the PDE problem. After addressing second-order parabolic equations, we explore how HTE is even more efficient in higher-order and higher-dimensional scenarios, which motivates the extension of HTE to the biharmonic equation.

Since the biharmonic equation is a fourth-order high-dimensional equation, solving it directly with conventional PINNs would lead to a massive tensor of size d^{4}, where d represents the dimensionality of the PDE problem and 4 denotes the order of the equation. However, by extending the Hessian Vector Product (HVP) in HTE to a tensor-vector product (TVP), we can transform the computation of the entire colossal tensor into a scalar, the TVP output. This not only saves a considerable amount of memory but also allows rapid computation using Taylor-mode differentiation. We also show that the extended HTE method provides an unbiased estimate for the biharmonic operator, and we analyze the sources of its variance. To emphasize the importance of properly implementing the HVP and TVP of HTE in JAX, we present a pseudocode to familiarize readers with HTE and its efficient implementation.

Finally, we showcase the effectiveness of HTE in various experimental setups. Firstly, we show that HTE and SDGD exhibit similar convergence rates under the same memory constraints and speed limitations on a second-order nonlinear anisotropic parabolic equation. Notably, they successfully scale PINNs to a very high dimension (100,000 dimensions). Secondly, we illustrate how HTE can accelerate the more accurate Gradient-Enhanced PINN (gPINN). Since gPINN requires additional first-order derivatives of the original PINN residual, its computational load is substantial, but HTE mitigates this burden while keeping the improvement brought by gPINN. Lastly, we highlight the advantages of HTE for higher-order, high-dimensional biharmonic equations.

This paper is arranged as follows. We present related work in Section 2. We then introduce the proposed HTE method in Section 3. We present computational experiments in Section 4 and summarize the paper in Section 5.
